questions.stem: A cyclone crosses an uninhabited stretch of the Kimberley coast and causes no losses to any community. It is best described as:
options: a hazard event that did not become a disaster
a disaster, because it reached cyclone strength at landfall
a technological hazard, because no people were involved
a biological hazard, because it affected only wildlife
questions.explanation: A hazard event becomes a disaster only when it seriously disrupts a community with losses. The cyclone was a hazard event of high magnitude, but magnitude alone does not make a disaster.

questions.stem: In Australian emergency management, the approach known as PPRR stands for:
options: prevention, preparedness, response and recovery
prediction, planning, rebuilding and reporting
protection, prevention, rescue and reconstruction
preparedness, policing, relief and resettlement
questions.explanation: PPRR describes the full cycle of managing hazards: prevention (and mitigation) before an event, preparedness, response during it and recovery afterwards. It is used by Australian and Victorian emergency agencies.

questions.stem: In hazard management, mitigation means:
options: actions taken before an event to reduce its likely impacts
the emergency rescue of people trapped during a hazard event
rebuilding homes and roads in the months after a disaster
measuring the magnitude of a hazard event once it has ended
questions.explanation: Mitigation reduces the severity of future impacts, for example through levees, building codes or planned burning. Rescue is part of the response phase, and rebuilding is recovery and reconstruction.

questions.stem: A household writing a bushfire survival plan before summer is an example of:
options: recovery and reconstruction
prediction of the hazard
emergency relief
community preparedness
questions.explanation: Preparedness means getting ready before a hazard event, for example by deciding when to leave and where to go. Relief and recovery happen during and after an event.

questions.stem: Rebuilding a washed-away road bridge to a higher flood standard in the year after a flood is best classed as:
options: emergency response
a community warning program
recovery and reconstruction
prediction of risk
questions.explanation: Work done after a disaster to restore infrastructure is recovery and reconstruction. Building to a higher standard also applies the idea of 'building back better', which reduces future risk.

questions.stem: Which is a non-structural response to the flood hazard?
options: raising the main road out of town onto a higher embankment
zoning floodplain land so that new homes cannot be built there
building an earth levee along the river bank right beside the town centre
constructing a retarding basin to hold back peak stormwater
questions.explanation: Non-structural responses reduce risk through planning, regulation, warnings and education rather than engineering works. In Victoria, overlays such as the Land Subject to Inundation Overlay control development on flood-prone land.

questions.stem: In Victorian planning schemes, the Bushfire Management Overlay is used to:
options: direct residents to evacuate their homes during a bushfire emergency
require bushfire protection measures for new development in high-risk areas
ban every type of residential building anywhere near state forest or bushland
set the dates on which the fire danger period begins in each municipality
questions.explanation: The overlay identifies land where the bushfire hazard is high and requires new buildings to include protection measures such as defendable space and water supply. It is land use planning, not an emergency warning tool.

questions.stem: After Cyclone Tracy devastated Darwin on Christmas Day 1974, a key long-term response was:
options: a new warning system for tsunamis approaching from the Indian Ocean
stronger building codes requiring homes to withstand cyclonic winds
the permanent relocation of the city of Darwin to a site far inland
a ban on building any new homes anywhere in northern Australia
questions.explanation: Darwin was rebuilt on the same site under much stricter wind-loading standards for houses. These building codes are a mitigation response that has reduced damage in later cyclones across northern Australia.

questions.stem: After a levee is built, new housing spreads onto the protected floodplain. Years later a larger flood overtops the levee, and damage is greater than before it was built. This best shows that:
options: flood risk depends only on the magnitude of a flood, not on where people live
the land use planning on the floodplain caused the larger flood to occur
a structural response can raise risk by encouraging development in exposed areas
levees always fail because they are non-structural responses to the flood hazard
questions.explanation: This is the 'levee effect': a sense of safety draws more people and property into the hazard zone, so losses are greater when protection is exceeded. Levees are structural responses, and planning cannot cause the flood itself.

questions.stem: A council builds a groyne at right angles to an eroding beach to trap sand moved by longshore drift. A likely issue arising from this response is:
options: the spread of invasive weeds across the dunes behind it
increased erosion on the beach down-drift of the groyne
increased erosion on the up-drift side, where sand builds up
a rise in sea level along the section of beach it protects
questions.explanation: A groyne traps sand on its up-drift side, so less sand reaches the beach beyond it, which then erodes faster. Responses can shift a problem along the coast rather than remove it.

questions.stem: For a coastal town facing rising seas, managed retreat differs from building a sea wall because managed retreat:
options: moves homes and assets away from the hazard over time
holds the present shoreline firmly in place with rock
adds sand to the beach to widen it after each storm
relies on warnings to evacuate residents during surges
questions.explanation: Managed retreat reduces exposure by relocating assets inland, accepting that the shoreline will move. Holding the line with rock is a sea wall, and adding sand is beach nourishment.

questions.stem: A council compares a sea wall and beach nourishment to protect a popular surf beach. Which statement correctly identifies an issue with each?
options: a sea wall causes sea levels to rise locally; nourishment permanently ends all erosion
a sea wall is a non-structural response; nourishment is a form of managed retreat
a sea wall can scour the beach in front of it; nourishment must be repeated as sand is lost
a sea wall needs topping up with sand after storms; nourishment reflects waves and scours
questions.explanation: Hard walls reflect wave energy, which can strip sand from the beach in front of them. Nourishment keeps a natural beach but is temporary, because waves and currents keep removing the added sand.

questions.stem: After the 2011 floods in Queensland's Lockyer Valley, residents of Grantham were offered land swaps on higher ground nearby. This response is an example of:
options: a biological control used to manage the floodplain
land use planning that reduces exposure to the flood hazard
a structural flood-control measure built across the valley
an early-warning program based on river gauge readings
questions.explanation: Moving homes off the floodplain removes them from the hazard zone, a planning response rather than an engineering one. It reduces risk for future floods, not just the one that occurred.

questions.stem: Which organisation issues flood and severe weather warnings across Australia?
options: the Australian Electoral Commission
the Bureau of Meteorology
the Australian Bureau of Statistics
the Reserve Bank of Australia
questions.explanation: The Bureau of Meteorology monitors rainfall and river levels and issues flood, severe weather and cyclone warnings. State agencies such as the SES then use these warnings to advise communities.

questions.stem: Emergency Alert, used by Australian emergency services, is a system that:
options: predicts the exact path of a fire days in advance
pays compensation to residents after a disaster
builds shelters in towns that face high risk
sends warnings to phones in a defined area at risk
questions.explanation: Emergency Alert sends voice messages to landlines and text messages to mobile phones in an area at risk. It is a warning tool, so it supports evacuation and preparedness rather than prediction or recovery.

questions.stem: To measure whether a new flood warning system has been effective, a geographer should compare:
options: evacuation times and losses in similar floods before and after it began
the number of warnings the system issued in its first year of operation
the cost of the new system with the cost of the old warning system
the rainfall totals recorded across the catchment in each recent year
questions.explanation: Effectiveness is judged by outcomes: whether people acted sooner and losses fell in comparable events. The number of warnings or the system's cost says nothing about whether it changed behaviour or reduced harm.

questions.stem: In a region where many warnings are followed by events that cause little damage, residents begin to ignore warnings. This challenge is best described as:
options: a strong spatial association between warnings and damage
warning fatigue, which reduces the effectiveness of future warnings
the levee effect, which increases the magnitude of later hazard events
a secondary hazard triggered by the warning system itself
questions.explanation: Warning fatigue erodes trust and response rates, so a later, serious warning may be ignored. The levee effect is about structural protection drawing development into hazard zones, not about warnings.

questions.stem: Some residents of a flood-prone town ignore evacuation orders because earlier floods never reached their homes. This shows how responses are influenced by:
options: past experiences and perceptions of the hazard
the economic capacity of the national government
the geological classification of the hazard type
the availability of geospatial technologies
questions.explanation: People's past experience shapes how they judge risk, and a 'my house has never flooded' perception can lead to dangerous decisions in a larger flood. Clear warnings and education aim to overcome this.

questions.stem: After Black Saturday in 2009, the Victorian Bushfires Royal Commission recommended changing the 'stay or go' policy. The main shift in advice was:
options: relying on aerial water bombing to protect towns instead of issuing warnings
greater emphasis on leaving early as the safest option on the worst days
advising all residents to stay and defend their homes regardless of conditions
ending all community bushfire warnings so residents rely on their own judgement
questions.explanation: The Royal Commission found that many homes could not be defended in extreme conditions and that leaving early is the safest choice. Warnings were strengthened rather than ended.

questions.stem: A challenge in using planned (fuel-reduction) burning to reduce bushfire risk is that:
options: it can be carried out only during the peak of the fire season
safe weather windows are limited, and smoke affects nearby residents
it permanently removes all vegetation from the forest that is burnt
it increases the fuel load available to the next bushfire in the area
questions.explanation: Planned burns need mild, stable weather, so the number of suitable days is limited, and smoke can harm health and the economy. Burns aim to reduce fuel, and they are done outside the peak season to keep them controllable.

questions.stem: Mapping shows that house losses in past bushfires cluster where homes back directly on to forest. A planning response that uses this spatial association is:
options: moving the region's fire station further from the forest
requiring defendable space between new homes and bushland
building more new homes directly against the forest edge
relying only on aerial firefighting to protect those homes
questions.explanation: The association between losses and proximity to forest supports requiring a cleared or managed buffer around new homes. Building closer to the forest would increase exposure.

questions.stem: A limitation of computer simulations that predict a bushfire's spread is that:
options: sudden wind changes and spot fires can make a fire behave differently from the model
they can be run only after a fire has finished burning and the damage has been mapped
they leave out the influence of wind, temperature and humidity on how a fire behaves
they cannot show the landscape on a map at any scale
questions.explanation: Fire models rely on forecast weather, fuel and terrain data, and real fires can change suddenly with wind shifts and embers. They are still useful for deciding which communities to warn first.

questions.stem: Base isolation reduces earthquake damage to a building by:
options: separating it from ground motion with flexible bearings
anchoring it rigidly to the bedrock so it cannot move
making its walls heavier so that it resists shaking
predicting the earthquake so the building is emptied
questions.explanation: Flexible bearings or pads between the building and its foundation absorb much of the ground's movement. Rigid, heavy structures attract greater forces and are more likely to crack.

questions.stem: Japan's earthquake early warning system can give seconds of warning before strong shaking arrives because it:
options: predicts the date and time of each earthquake several days in advance by counting the foreshocks
measures the tides to detect changes in sea level before each earthquake
uses satellites to see the fault move before the rocks actually break
detects the faster, weaker P-waves before the damaging S-waves and surface waves arrive
questions.explanation: P-waves travel faster than the more damaging waves, and electronic alerts travel faster still, so places away from the epicentre get seconds of warning. No system can yet predict the time of an earthquake in advance.

questions.stem: Before the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, many coastal communities had no warning. A key global response afterwards was:
options: the relocation of all coastal villages in the region to inland sites
an Indian Ocean tsunami warning system using seismic and sea-level sensors
the construction of sea walls along every coastline of the Indian Ocean
a ban on building tourist resorts in all coastal areas of the region
questions.explanation: Countries around the Indian Ocean, coordinated through UNESCO's Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission, built a warning system linking seismometers, sea-level gauges and national warning centres. Australia contributes through its Joint Australian Tsunami Warning Centre.

questions.stem: Japan had high sea walls and well-practised drills before the 2011 tsunami, yet the tsunami overtopped walls in many towns. The best conclusion about these responses is that:
options: drills increase risk because they make residents too confident to evacuate
they reduced losses, but structures can be exceeded, so warnings and evacuation remain vital
they had no value at all, so coastal defences should now be abandoned in every country
sea walls work only against storm surges, and never against a tsunami of any height at all
questions.explanation: Evaluating effectiveness means weighing benefits against limits: walls slowed and reduced the water in places, while evacuation saved many lives where walls were overtopped. A response can be partly effective without being complete protection.

questions.stem: Inspecting cargo and travellers' luggage at Australia's borders is a response to biological hazards that aims mainly at:
options: predicting where existing pests will spread
rebuilding habitats damaged by invasive species
preventing new pests and diseases from entering
helping farmers recover after an outbreak ends
questions.explanation: Biosecurity at the border is prevention: it is far cheaper to stop a pest arriving than to control it once established. Australia's quarantine rules on food, plants and animals serve this purpose.

questions.stem: Releasing a rust fungus that attacks only blackberry plants is an example of:
options: land use zoning
biological control
mechanical control
chemical control
questions.explanation: Biological control uses a living natural enemy to suppress a pest. Mechanical control removes plants by hand or machine, and chemical control uses herbicides.

questions.stem: The myxoma virus, released in 1950, first cut Australia's rabbit numbers dramatically, but its effect weakened over the following decades. The main reason was that:
options: the virus also killed the rabbits' main native predators
farmers stopped all other rabbit control once it was released
the virus could survive only in the far north of Australia
rabbits evolved resistance and less lethal virus strains spread
questions.explanation: Natural selection favoured resistant rabbits, and milder virus strains that let hosts live longer spread more easily. This is why rabbit calicivirus was later released as a further biological control.

questions.stem: Community 'toad-busting' musters that collect and humanely kill cane toads have limited effect on toad numbers at a regional scale because:
options: toads live only in remote deserts that people cannot reach
toads breed so prolifically that removal cannot keep pace
cane toads are protected native animals that cannot be killed
the musters attract more toads from other parts of Australia
questions.explanation: A single female can lay many thousands of eggs, so local removal is quickly offset. Musters can still protect particular sites and raise community awareness, which is part of evaluating a response's effectiveness.

questions.stem: Which global organisation can declare a public health emergency of international concern?
options: the World Health Organization
the World Trade Organization
the International Monetary Fund
the World Meteorological Organization
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization coordinates the international response to disease outbreaks and can declare such an emergency. This triggers advice to countries on how to respond.

questions.stem: After the Exxon Valdez spill, the United States required new oil tankers in its waters to have double hulls. This response mainly aims to:
options: predict which tankers are most likely to run aground on reefs
make spilled oil break down faster once it is in the water
reduce the chance that a grounding or collision releases oil
speed up the clean-up of oil that has already reached the coast
questions.explanation: A second inner hull means a breach of the outer hull is less likely to release cargo, so it prevents spills rather than cleaning them up. It is an example of a response changing after a major hazard event.

questions.stem: Chemical dispersants break oil slicks into tiny droplets that mix into the water. A key issue with this response is that it:
options: can be used only on oil that has already washed up on sandy beaches
turns the oil into fresh water that dilutes the surrounding seawater
moves oil from the surface into the water column rather than removing it
makes the slick thicker and harder for skimmers to collect at the surface
questions.explanation: Dispersants protect shorelines and seabirds at the surface, but the oil and chemicals remain in the sea, where they can harm fish, plankton and coral. Booms and skimmers remove oil, while dispersants only redistribute it.

questions.stem: Bangladesh's cyclone preparedness program has greatly reduced deaths from cyclones since the 1970s, despite the country's limited wealth. This has been achieved mainly through:
options: building a continuous sea wall that stops every storm surge
preventing cyclones from forming over the Bay of Bengal
warning volunteers, cyclone shelters and community evacuation plans
moving the entire coastal population permanently to the capital city
questions.explanation: Trained volunteers spread warnings, and shelters give people somewhere safe to go, showing that low-cost community measures can be very effective. Cyclones and surges still occur; the response reduces their human impact.

questions.stem: After the same hurricane, insured homeowners in a suburb rebuilt within a year, while uninsured renters in the same suburb were displaced for years. This shows that:
options: the hurricane's magnitude was greater for the renters' homes
recovery depends only on the physical size of the hazard event
renters were exposed to a secondary biological hazard instead
economic factors shape how quickly different groups recover
questions.explanation: With the same hazard in the same place, the difference comes from economic capacity such as insurance and savings. Responses must consider vulnerable groups, or recovery can widen inequality.

questions.stem: Which is a political factor that can weaken the response to a disaster?
options: a cultural tradition of extended families sheltering each other
a heavy wet season that floods the roads used by relief trucks
conflict or corruption that stops aid from reaching survivors
a steep mountain landscape that blocks road access to towns
questions.explanation: Governance, conflict and corruption affect whether resources reach the people who need them. Terrain and weather are environmental factors, and family support is a cultural factor that often helps recovery.

questions.stem: During the Millennium Drought, Victoria built a desalination plant near Wonthaggi. A main issue raised about this response was:
options: it reduced Melbourne's water supply during the drought years
it drew all of its water from the rivers of the Murray–Darling
it caused the drought across Victoria to last several years longer
its high cost and energy use, as it was not needed in wet years
questions.explanation: Desalination gives a supply independent of rainfall, but it is expensive and energy-intensive, and the plant was not called on for some years after the drought broke. The plant takes in seawater from Bass Strait, not river water.

questions.stem: The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 is:
options: a Japanese system for issuing earthquake early warnings to residents
a scale used for measuring the magnitude of earthquakes
a United Nations agreement to reduce disaster risk and losses
an Australian law that sets building codes in bushfire areas
questions.explanation: The Sendai Framework, adopted by UN member states, sets targets to reduce disaster deaths, losses and damage. It shifts focus from responding to disasters towards reducing risk before they happen.

questions.stem: In disaster recovery, the principle of 'build back better' means:
options: using reconstruction to make communities more resilient than before
rebuilding exactly what was lost, in the same place, as fast as possible
replacing local recovery decisions with those of international agencies
delaying all rebuilding until the hazard can no longer occur again
questions.explanation: Build back better, promoted in the Sendai Framework, uses recovery to reduce future risk, for example with stronger buildings or safer sites. Rebuilding exactly what was there can recreate the same vulnerability.

questions.stem: Flood maps made from LiDAR elevation data help planners mainly by:
options: giving the names and ages of the residents of each flooded home
stopping floodwater from reaching homes on the mapped floodplain
showing which land would be inundated at different flood heights
measuring the rainfall that fell during each past flood event
questions.explanation: LiDAR produces a detailed digital elevation model, so the area covered at each water level can be modelled. Planners then use these maps for zoning and emergency plans.

questions.stem: During a bushfire, a GIS combining predicted fire spread with road and population layers helps agencies to:
options: decide which communities to warn first and which roads to close
guarantee that no homes in the fire's path will be destroyed
remove the fuel from the landscape ahead of the fire front
replace the need for firefighters to attend the fire ground
questions.explanation: Overlaying layers shows where the fire is likely to meet people and escape routes, supporting timely warnings and traffic management. GIS informs decisions but does not itself stop damage.

questions.stem: The International Charter 'Space and Major Disasters' provides satellite images of disaster zones to emergency agencies. Its greatest value in the response is that:
options: the images prevent secondary hazards from occurring after the main event
the images remove the need for any field checks of the damage by crews working on the ground
the images predict the exact date of the next disaster in the same region
before-and-after images show the extent of damage over wide or inaccessible areas
questions.explanation: Comparing images from before and after an event lets agencies see damage quickly where roads are cut or areas are large. Field checks are still needed to confirm conditions on the ground.
